problem: Traditional closed-set object detectors cannot handle open-ended object search where the target is specified by language, and prior open-vocabulary navigation work is mostly simulation-only and too heavy for resource-constrained robots.
motivation: Service robotics, warehouse automation and disaster response need robots that find arbitrary user-specified objects in unknown environments. Such robots have to run on embedded hardware in real time.
key_idea: Combine frontier-based exploration and RTABMap SLAM with a language-driven open-vocabulary detector (Grounding DINO), and use depth-based coordinate estimation to navigate to the detected object on an embedded UGV.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so the ablations are not visible. The abstract reports that Grounding DINO outperforms the YOLO-World baseline by 13.1 percentage points in F1 in real-world demonstrations. It also claims the pipeline can be ported to an Orin Nano at about 1 Hz.
method: Frontier-based exploration: the robot autonomously explores unknown space by choosing frontiers.
RTABMap SLAM: provides real-time localization, mapping and dynamic navigation.
Open-vocabulary detection: a language-driven detector (Grounding DINO, compared against YOLO-World) detects objects specified by a natural language query.
Depth-based localization: the detected object's 3D coordinates are estimated from depth, and the robot navigates to that location.
Edge deployment: the model is ported to a Jetson Orin Nano and runs at about 1 Hz on the AgileX LIMO UGV.

setting.backbone: Grounding DINO (open-vocabulary detector, pretrained); YOLO-World as a baseline
setting.action_space: navigation goals to frontiers and object locations via a ROS-style planner, executed as continuous velocity commands on a UGV

numbers_note: abstract only; the abstract reports 100% precision/recall for small objects (screws/kettles), 91.3% chair precision, 95.5% average F1, and +13.1 points over YOLO-World, but these are not tied to a canonical benchmark table.
results: Real-world experiments on the AgileX LIMO report 100% precision/recall for small objects (screws, kettles), 91.3% chair detection precision in clutter, and an average F1 of 95.5%. This is 13.1 points above the YOLO-World baseline. The system runs at about 1 Hz on an Orin Nano.
limitations: Only about 1 Hz inference on the edge device, which limits reactivity.
Evaluation is a small set of real-world demonstrations with detection metrics rather than standard navigation benchmarks (SR/SPL).
Relies on the detector's accuracy and on depth quality.
